evidence_levels.Model: Software run without the key: product code with the mock signer standing in for it, or a model of a rule. Most of these cases ran in Windows or Linux virtual machines. Not firmware or a device.
evidence_levels.Simulated: Chrome with a virtual authenticator and a local test site. Not a device or CTAP firmware.
evidence_levels.Synthetic page: A scripted test page in Chrome. Not a real website.
evidence_levels.Hardware: A real device. None exists yet.
evidence_levels.Host software: Real Linux-PAM and pam_u2f libraries run in a private configuration with synthetic fallback modules. Not a real login surface, a device or CTAP firmware.

Firefox passkey inside an embedded frame in v0.5, Debian 13 GNOME and Windows 11

N36 untested-02, 25 November 2026. The v0.5 installer does not set Firefox up. On Debian it printed only registered the native messaging host for Google Chrome and left no .mozilla folder. On Windows it registered Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge and left the Mozilla native messaging key empty. The extension manifest has a background service_worker and no Firefox settings. A probe page showed that Firefox 153.7 ESR on Debian and Firefox 160 on Windows expose neither document.permissionsPolicy nor document.featurePolicy inside a frame, while Chromium exposes featurePolicy. The extension code refuses a passkey request in any frame when there is no policy object, so even if it were set up the request would be refused, as recorded in R49. The extension was never run in Firefox and nothing was loaded to work around this, so the refusal is from the probe and from reading the code. The page used for Windows was served from a non local address, so PublicKeyCredential also showed as undefined there, because Firefox hides it outside secure contexts. No passkey was attempted in Firefox.
